title: Molecular clock ages of component groups in individual distribution patterns form surprisingly smooth curves: does vicariance never occur, or are the clock ages wrong?
content:
Abstract
Molecular studies have dated many component clades in particular biogeographical patterns. Here we review age curves for clades in different patterns, worldwide. Any vicariance would cause multiple, unrelated clades in a pattern to have the same age. However, calculated ages for the biotas of many regions form surprisingly smooth curves, with no pulses, implying that either vicariance never occurs, or that the clock ages are wrong. Vicariance is now widely accepted as an important process in biogeography, and so the first option seems unlikely. The clade ages in molecular studies are mostly fossil-calibrated and converted into estimates of clade age by imposing Bayesian priors. However, the priors, selection of which is usually arbitrary and subjective, specify how much older a clade can be than its oldest fossil, and the practice has been criticised as lacking rigor. While the fossil-calibrated clade ages can be very precise and have strong statistical support, studies using biogeographical–tectonic dating suggest that they could be incorrect by tens of millions of years. The smooth curves for the clade ages in a particular pattern probably result from bias in the fossil record: a younger fossil is more likely to survive until the present, and be found and documented.
